message.content:
**Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024)** | Area | Key Points | What You Should Do | |------|------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **$1,000** for a single‑unit rental.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Keep a copy of the lease and a move‑in inspection report. Document any existing damage before moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the property safe, clean, and in good repair.
• Must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural integrity. | Report problems promptly in writing. If unresolved, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (but only after giving written notice). | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: **30‑day** written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: follow the lease’s end date; no extra notice needed unless you’re breaking it early. | Use certified mail or a reliable delivery service to prove notice was received. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent.
• Must give **30 days’ written notice** for increases. | Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **30‑day** notice for nonpayment or a **60‑day** notice for other violations.
• After notice, the landlord files an unlawful detainer action in court.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | Keep all correspondence. Attend the hearing if you receive a summons. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Property Code §92.001.
• Discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap is illegal. | File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights if you suspect discrimination. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord must give **24 hours’ notice** before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | Ask for a written entry log if you’re concerned about frequent visits. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may repair them yourself and deduct the cost from rent (after giving written notice). | Keep receipts and document the problem. | | **Lease Termination** | • You can break a lease for “just cause” (e.g., landlord’s failure to maintain habitability).
• You may also terminate if the landlord violates your rights. | Provide written notice and evidence of the violation. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division.
• Texas Legal Services Center.
• Local tenant unions or advocacy groups. | Contact them for free or low‑cost legal advice. | --- ### Quick Checklist Before Moving Out 1. **Review Lease** – Note any special clauses (pet deposits, subletting, etc.). 2. **Move‑In Inspection** – Compare photos or notes taken at move‑in. 3. **Document Condition** – Take dated photos/video of each room. 4. **Written Notice** – Send a 30‑day notice via certified mail. 5. **Final Walk‑Through** – Schedule a walk‑through with the landlord. 6. **Return Keys** – Hand over all keys and locksets. 7. **Request Deposit Return** – Ask for a written statement of any deductions. --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a habitable home, timely return of your security deposit, proper notice for rent changes or termination, protection against discrimination, and the ability to contest unlawful evictions. Keep records, communicate in writing, and know where to seek help if your landlord violates your rights.
